Business.title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal
Business.text:
Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.

Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.

Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.

Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.

Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.

“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”

Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.

There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration has scrambled to respond to the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.

“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.

For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have also made recent advancements that could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.

It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stock selloff in July wiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.

Business.title: Dutch central bank moves 86 tonnes of gold to UK from US and Canada, citing ‘geopolitical unrest’
Business.text:
The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.

“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.

“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.

The total Dutch gold stock amounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.

Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.

After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.

The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold in the Netherlands.

The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.

The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.

The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.

“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.

The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.

“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.

The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.

“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”

John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.

For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.

At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.

However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.

“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.

Sports.title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners
Sports.text:
Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.

Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.

While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.

Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.

After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.

Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.

A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up.

"I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.

It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.

But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.

Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.

After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.

Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead.

"Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time.

"We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant.

"We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."

Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term.

"It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.

Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season.

"He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport.

"He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball.

"The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way.

"Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team.

"It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."

Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best".

"He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward.

"He's going to help us a lot this season."

Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window.

"They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker.

"Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."

Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.

They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.

Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.

Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.

Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea.

"Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final.

"We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."

Sports.title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Are Blues short of midfield options despite £349m spent?
Sports.text:
Chelsea ended Sunday's 2-1 defeat by champions Arsenal with two players who began their careers as right-backs alongside each other in midfield.

After spending £349m during the summer transfer window, how did they reach that point?

It was Reece James, who began his career as a right-back, who failed to track captain Martin Odegaard as he scored Arsenal's winner at Emirates Stadium.

In the build-up to his first defeat as Chelsea manager, Xabi Alonso said he believes James can become one of the best midfielders in the world.

James performed well otherwise and spent almost half of last season playing in midfield.

But there are legitimate questions about Chelsea's depth in that area after Malo Gusto replaced midfielder Romeo Lavia in the second half.

It was lax marking that led to Odegaard's winner, while a lack of creativity from the bench left Chelsea short as Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's substitutes ultimately helped guide the hosts to victory.

"Chelsea don't have European football this season so they're playing less games and can concentrate on the Premier League. But the worry is you're finishing a game against the champions, and you've got two right-backs in midfield," Ashley Young told BBC Sport.

"You look at Lavia, who was injured a lot last season. The front line are going to send fear throughout the league but behind that you see the midfield and they're playing right-backs there.

"Teams will be seeing the game today, seeing that Chelsea will sit in there and get men behind the ball, but there's still spaces through the lines, and Arsenal found that out.

"Chelsea are giving up a lot of possession and they're playing counter-attacking football. Today there was probably only once with [Pedro] Neto down the right side when they capitalised on the counter."

The primary issue is the absence of midfielder Moises Caicedo.

The Ecuador international is out with an unspecified injury for an unknown period after breaking down just 11 minutes into a substitute appearance against Brighton last week.

It has left Alonso in almost uncharted territory for a Chelsea boss. Aside from suspensions, Caicedo had missed only two matches during the previous three seasons, through a knock and illness.

Asked about Caicedo, Alonso said: "Not longer term, but it is about assessing the risk. Probably last week we brought him back too early and I don't want to make the same mistake again."

It remains unclear whether Chelsea had concerns over Caicedo's fitness while pursuing several central midfielders on transfer deadline day.

Monaco pulled the plug on Chelsea's £47m move for Lamine Camara at the last minute, leaving officials at Stamford Bridge furious.

Chelsea also had bids of up to £64m rejected for Bournemouth's Alex Scott earlier in the summer and were prevented from signing France international Manu Kone after Roma head coach Gian Piero Gasperini blocked the move.

Chelsea said they pursued Camara because of a market opportunity, adding that they were satisfied with their summer business and retained faith in their current options.

That was despite selling Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City for a joint British-record fee of £125m on deadline day, without signing a direct replacement.

However, Caicedo's absence means he joins Jordan Henderson on the sidelines, with the England international still recovering from a broken arm suffered after falling over an advertising hoarding while an unused substitute at the World Cup.

Natural midfielder Valentin Barco, who joined from Strasbourg in the summer, has been overlooked in favour of Gusto in all three of Chelsea's Premier League matches.

With Gusto starting in midfield, Chelsea recorded 25.6% possession in last weekend's 4-3 victory over Brighton, their lowest figure since records began in 2003-04.

If all of Chelsea's midfield options are fit, and Caicedo's injury proves only minor, they should be able to cope with five midfielders in a season without midweek European football, as Alonso argued before the match.

Chelsea have leaned on their star attackers in Morgan Rogers, a resurgent Cole Palmer and the prolific Joao Pedro in their opening three matches.

Yet having conceded seven goals in three matches, Alonso said "we want to be tighter".

There was still plenty to admire about Chelsea's performance.

Club-record signing Rogers scored again in the second minute, becoming the first Chelsea player to score or assist in each of the club's opening three Premier League matches of a season since Eden Hazard in 2018-19.

It was arguably one of Chelsea's better performances against Arsenal during a run of 10 matches without a win against their London rivals.

There remains a 33-point gap to make up after Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season.

Alonso said after the match: "We came to win. We knew that we were not that far, but it went their way.

"It hurts, [we're] disappointed for sure. But this is the first defeat, this is going to be a long way and it doesn't have a big impact in our mood and in our mindset."

Arsenal remain the benchmark Chelsea are trying to reach. Although the Blues beat them to the signing of Rogers, they still trail the standard-setters in London and the Premier League.

It served to highlight that, despite already recruiting 10 first-team players during a busy summer, Chelsea's failure to sign a midfielder on deadline day may have left them with a potential weakness.

Alonso described the summer as "phase one" earlier this week. If Caicedo's return does not resolve Chelsea's midfield issues, the club may face questions over its decision not to sign a replacement for Fernandez before turning back to the market in January.

Sports.title: Italian Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli's stunning Monza victory will go down in F1 folklore
Sports.text:
Kimi Antonelli's stunning victory in the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid will go down in Formula 1 folklore - and, remarkably, his team boss Toto Wolff said that he had seen it coming on Saturday.

After Sunday's race, Wolff said that beforehand he thought that one of his two drivers was going to be standing on the top of the podium.

It was an eye-opening statement given they started the race 17 places apart on the grid, George Russell on the front row alongside shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine; Antonelli on the penultimate row.

"I thought one of the two is going to win," Wolff said. "Either George, because he was on the front row, or Kimi because he's going to walk over water, here at Monza. And I felt that yesterday also."

Wolff was asked to explain why he felt a performance he was comparing to a miracle was on the cards.

"It's been a while that I've seen drivers," he said. "Energy levels, mindset or behavioural pattern. I knew that was his mission today, to win the race. I chatted with his father yesterday. The father also saw that coming.

"These are the moments where you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions that a special moment can come."

For the Mercedes drivers, this race was all about the context of the weekend.

Antonelli knew coming in that he would be starting at the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engines this year.

Russell knew that he had to make the most of this opportunity and cut as much as he could out of his team-mate's 59-point championship lead.

Fifth or sixth was the general consensus for what might be realistically possible for Antonelli, who himself said after the race that he had "thought a podium was possible".

What changed everything was his remarkable progress in the early laps of the race, which brought to mind another Biblical miracle, the parting of the Red Sea.

Antonelli was 14th after a relatively conservative first lap, then 12th at the end of lap two, when Charles Leclerc crashed his Ferrari to bring the race to a temporary halt.

"With the red flag, I was already P12," Antonelli said. "And then I knew that I could have a shot at it."

A lap after the restart, he was up to eighth, and on the back of the leading group of cars running nose to tail. Seventh a lap later, after dispatching Lando Norris' McLaren.

By now, Russell was in the lead, having wasted little time dispensing with Gasly. But the Briton sensed trouble.

"A great race from the neutral perspective," Russell said. "As soon as I saw Kimi up to P5 after a handful of laps, I knew he was going to be in the fight with us. That was clearly a very impressive opening few laps."

Wolff said: "The differentiator today was the ability to go through the traffic. We've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis (Hamilton), who did it in some of the races. That's what he's shown today. When a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them."

Briefly, for a few laps, Russell and Max Verstappen threatened to break away in the lead while Antonelli was finding a way past Gasly, the two McLarens and Hamilton's Ferrari.

But Russell and Verstappen were fighting at the front, costing each other time, and Antonelli was up to third by lap 13, just 1.8secs off Verstappen in the lead, with Russell between them.

Three laps later, the Mercedes drivers were running one-two, and starting to swap places themselves, until, with Russell leading, it was suggested by that team that they give it a rest and try to break away from Verstappen.

If Russell could not do so, they said, they would "invert the cars" - put Antonelli into the lead to try himself. But slowly they began to inch clear.

At this point, coming up to half-distance, the race victory was still up in the air. There was a virtual safety car (VSC), called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first corner.

Mercedes called Antonelli for new tyres - a decision they had to make as he had switched to the medium compound at the red flag and that would not make it to the end. Russell continued on his hard tyres.

"It was the right thing to split the strategies," Wolff said, "because we didn't know what the better one would be. In the morning meeting, we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it. And you can see with George, it was a forever tyre.

"At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead, that two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."

Antonelli was in no mood to obey a computer algorithm. Rejoining 14.3secs behind Russell, with 24 laps to go and four cars between them, winning was not an easy task. But he made it look like it.

Antonelli caught Russell with five laps to go and the win now looked inevitable. There was a hiccup when he ran off the track at turn one with four laps to go after Russell blocked his attack on the inside, and Antonelli lost grip on the loose rubber off line and slid into the gravel trap.

That dropped him to 1.7secs off again, but a lap and a half later, he drove past Russell on the straight between the second Lesmo corner and Ascari, and that was that.

The home fans, with split loyalties before the race between Antonelli and Ferrari, screamed with delight as he crossed the line, 60 years since the last time an Italian won his home race.

"It's one that I will remember forever," Antonelli said. "Definitely the fans gave that little bit extra to push more. The support has been great this weekend.

"Definitely seeing the grandstand cheering every lap it gave that little bit of extra to push more and to try and do even better to win it."

After the race, Russell tried to put a brave face on it, but it was impossible not to see how much it was hurting him.

Speaking in the news conference, sentences ran out of steam, his voice was on the point of breaking at times.

Russell gently pointed out, in not quite so many words, that without the VSC he probably would have won - "it would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC".

But he was well aware of what Antonelli's stellar performance meant. The strategy, he said, "takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether".

And the championship, he now knows, is almost a lost cause. Antonelli's win moves him 66 points clear.

Russell talked about "taking the positives", about how, after a "very tough run" in the early summer, since the season re-started in the Netherlands two weeks ago, "every lap, every session, I've been sort of in the mix of the top three positions, similar to where I was at the start of the year".

That's true. But there has not been a hint all year of Russell being able to put together a run of results where he consistently beats Antonelli, which is now his only hope.

"It's definitely Kimi's in control of it," Russell said. "And, you know, he's deserving to be in control of it.

"For me personally, I'm not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything. I'm just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend.

"He's performing incredibly well. It's going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. So I'm just sort of accepting that is what it is."

Sports.title: England v Ireland: Sophia Dunkley cetury seals hosts' dominant series clean sweep
Sports.text:
Third ODI, New Road, Worcester

England 291 (48.5 overs): Dunkley 119 (119); Murray 4-56

Ireland 177 (44.2 overs): Hunter 39 (58); Filer 3-27

England won by 114 runs; win series 3-0

Sophia Dunkley's sparkling century led England to a comprehensive 114-run win in the third and final one-day international against Ireland at Worcester.

Dunkley's run-a-ball 119 set up England's 291 before Ireland were bowled out for 177 in 44.2 overs, sealing a 3-0 clean sweep for Charlie Dean's side.

England were eyeing a record total after opener Dunkley's second international century, but the innings fell away from 260-4 and they frustratingly lost their last six wickets for just 31 runs to be dismissed with seven balls unused.

Dunkley added 73 for the first wicket with Maia Bouchier, who continued her fine run of form with 39, before Jodi Grewcock also wasted a good start as she was caught and bowled for 35 and Alice Capsey was unlucky to be run out backing up for 10.

All-rounders Freya Kemp and Dani Gibson threatened to push England beyond 300 but it was the former's wicket that kickstarted the collapse as she was caught at long-on for 23 and a run of single-figure scores followed, though Gibson kicked on to an ODI-best 41.

Leg-spinner Cara Murray was the pick of Ireland's bowlers with 4-56 as the visitors fought back admirably, and England only managed to hit seven boundaries after Dunkley's departure in the 36th over.

Despite the disappointing end to the innings, England still had plenty on the board in another non-contest between bat and ball.

Amy Hunter top-scored with 39 but no Irish batter was able to score at a strike-rate above 100 and the run-rate spiralled beyond their grasp, as Mady Villiers and Lauren Filer took three wickets apiece.

The final match of the series concludes England's international summer. Their next confirmed games will come at the Champions Trophy in February, though a multi-format series against West Indies in the autumn and three ODIs against Sri Lanka are in the schedule, but the dates have not been released.

This has been a series with an unusual context for England.

Key stars such as Lauren Bell, Sophie Ecclestone and Nat Sciver-Brunt have been rested, which has presented opportunities to experiment with the likes of fringe players in Grewcock and Tilly Corteen-Coleman.

But the curious cricketing calendar means they have few opportunities to play the format, with the autumn schedule still unconfirmed and their next home ODI coming in the Ashes next summer, meaning they have been simultaneously seeking stability.

The opening partnership was one question that needed answering after Tammy Beaumont's retirement earlier this year, and a century apiece for Dunkley and Bouchier in this series has seen them take their chance.

Of course, Ireland's bowling attack is incomparable to Australia's and to cite this as Ashes preparation would be very unrealistic, but England can only play the schedule they are given.

Dunkley had been threatening in the first two games, falling for 73 at Leicester before she was stitched up by Bouchier's poor running at Derby - but she was not to be denied a third time.

The 28-year-old started patiently, reaching her half-century off 63 balls after Bouchier dominated the strike early on, before kicking on and whacking her next fifty off just 37.

A notable change to her game has been her improvement through the off-side, scoring her runs almost equally split across both sides of the wicket - a big change for a player previously known for her leg-side dominance.

Ireland tested her with the short ball and forced her to hit to the sweepers, which she handled efficiently before her eventual downfall as she was brilliantly caught by Prendergast at deep square leg.

Sciver-Brunt is likely to slot straight back in at number three, and England have a decision to make about whether Capsey keeps the gloves over Amy Jones, but for now, Dunkley and Bouchier have solved one of coach Charlotte Edwards' headaches.

Sports.title: Troy Deeney's Team of the Week: Alexander Isak, Ezri Konsa, Tyrick Mitchell, Harvey Barnes
Sports.text:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Tell us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): Solid performance. He comes in again and just makes that massive tackle on Morgan Rogers. I think he slots into what is an already incredible Arsenal team. I can see a position now that they just can't live without him, he'll have to play right-back when everybody comes fit and available.

Ronald Araujo (Liverpool): I've given him a bit of stick for his games at Barcelona and his ability to not defend properly, because he's normally the one who's really aggressive. But I have to give it to him, he's been really good for Liverpool and played at right-back in that situation.

Tyrick Mitchell (Crystal Palace): Two goals from left-back. He deserves to be in any team of the week. He came off as well, but he's just Mr Consistent. He's never really spoken about enough.

Harvey Barnes (Newcastle): Gets a goal. Good finish into that far corner as well. He's been excellent and not spoken about a lot. Anthony Elanga and all the others get the headlines, but Barnes has been fantastic.

Martin Odegaard (Arsenal): Captain, leader and a massive winner. It's just one of those moments where you just think, how did they talk about getting rid of Odegaard? It's scary.

Cody Gakpo (Liverpool): Two goals created from midfield. Imagine thinking you're playing for Spurs and then for Man City, and then somehow you have to stay at Liverpool and compose yourself, and still perform.

Cesar Palacios (Fulham) and Vitaly Janelt (Brentford): Both very similar: solid and get the job done. They don't really get noticed in games unless they score, but if you're watching and you've played the game, you know these two are really important.

Alexander Isak (Liverpool): The guy they keep telling you isn't good. They say last year he wasn't good, even though he had two injuries, one being a broken leg. This season, he doesn't score in one game against Newcastle and, 'oh, he's not good enough, he's bottled it'. Just remember, someone tipped him for the Golden Boot.

Kai Havertz (Arsenal): The best striker for Arsenal, hands down. They keep telling us that Gyokeres will come good, but Havertz is their best striker. He proves it week in, week out. He's the best footballer they've got, and also their best finisher.

Sports.title: Man City: Iliman Ndiaye says 'you don't say no' when City want you
Sports.text:
Iliman Ndiaye says "you don't say no" when Manchester City come calling, and playing in the Champions League is where he belongs.

The 26-year-old could have gone to Tottenham but made a £60m move from Everton to City on transfer deadline day and was thrown straight into the starting XI for his new side in a 1-0 Premier League victory over Coventry at the weekend.

In the final week of the transfer window, it appeared as though Ndiaye would be moving to Spurs after they agreed a deal with Everton, but they were unable to proceed with the move having failed to sell Richarlison.

"There was no stress or panicking," said Ndiaye.

"I always say whatever comes, comes. God decides your future - it is already written.

"I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing. It was always going to be City.

"I wanted Champions League and playing at one of the best teams in the world. I am not saying Tottenham is not, but when Manchester City comes through you don't say no.

"It has been a good week for me and topped off with a win."

Despite Everton finishing in the bottom half of the table in his two seasons at the club, Ndiaye became a fans' favourite for his skills on the flanks and scoring 17 goals.

"When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her that if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League," he said.

Sports.title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beats Tommy Paul to reach quarter-finals
Sports.text:
Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.

Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4.

He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and his quarter-final opponent will be either American eighth seed Ben Shelton or Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas.

A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer.

He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18.

Asked on court if he is back to "full power", Alcaraz smiled as he replied: "I think so. Except for one year since [his US Open debut in] 2021, I've made the quarter-finals here. That shows how special this place is to me and shows how well I'm playing every time I come here.

"I just try to enjoy my time on the court and it doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months - every time I come here, I play my best."

Shelton and Tsitsipas meet in Sunday's night session and seven-time major champion Alcaraz has never previously lost to either player at Tour level, beating Shelton three times and Tsitsipas on six occasions.

"If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra.

"It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine."

Alcaraz said after his third-round win that he was happy with the level of fitness he had shown in the early rounds following his lengthy absence, while he demonstrated against Paul that the quality of his shot-making is as good as ever.

One sensational cross-court forehand winner early in the second set, which landed in from an almost impossible angle, was measured at 103mph.

That came shortly after Alcaraz had broken Paul's serve in the 10th game of a tight, high-quality opening set to take it 6-4.

Paul, who was attempting to reach the quarter-finals of his home Grand Slam for the first time, battled hard throughout but Alcaraz proved to be too strong.

Paul had two break points when Alcaraz served for the match at 5-4 in the third set, but the two-time US Open champion put together a run of four straight points to seal victory.

Former British number one Tim Henman told Sky Sports: "When you haven't played tennis for four weeks, it seems a lot and you can be a bit rusty. This is four and a half months.

"If you would have given Alcaraz a blank piece of paper at the beginning of the tournament and asked how he'd want the first four matches to go, he would have scripted it exactly like that.

"He's had a few slightly challenging moments but, in the important moments, he's just come up with incredible tennis. That's got to give him so much confidence moving forward."

Later on Sunday, home hope Frances Tiafoe delighted American fans with a entertaining victory over 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev.

Tiafoe saved a set point in the third-set tie-break before wrapping up a 7-6 (7-1) 6-4 7-6 (8-6) win moments later to maintain his perfect record on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

The 11th seed has won all 10 of his matches on the US Open's secondary show court, while it is just his second win in eight appearances against Russian Medvedev.

Tiafoe, a two-time semi-finalist in New York, will face fellow American Alex Michelsen in the last eight after the 22-year-old beat Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-4 to reach his first Grand Slam quarter-final.

Sports.title: Everton 2-2 Manchester United: Red Devils frustrated but Michael Carrick still optimistic
Sports.text:
There are positives for Manchester United to take from their 2-2 draw at Everton.

Striker Benjamin Sesko scored his first goal of a season - the start to which has been delayed for longer than anticipated by a shin injury.

Kobbie Mainoo has impressed in the campaign as a whole so far and shows no sign of being affected by his unhappy World Cup experience. The same, in terms of his mental strength, could be said of goakeeper Senne Lammens.

Marcus Rashford has returned to the club with a sense of purpose.

But you cannot ignore the negatives.

After a European based pre-season that should have seen them hit the ground running, Michael Carrick's side have dropped five points from their first three Premier League games.

They have conceded twice in all three. Their opponents are two promoted teams and an Everton outfit whose fans are distraught following a botched deadline day.

Now United must prepare for their Champions League return, against another banana skin-type opponent in Azerbaijan's Sabah FK. After that it is Manchester City.

It is the kind of week they craved 12 months ago. But already, the pressure is on.

"It's not that bad, you know," was Carrick's assessment of his side's start to the season.

"We were that close to coming away with three points today. That's football. There were little moments we can deal with a bit better, but we'll be fine."

Carrick got support in his assessment from his old friend Wayne Rooney, who analysed the Everton game for BBC Sport.

"I thought it was good away performance," he said.

"Obviously, I'd be disappointed with the result, but I thought there was a lot more control in the performance.

"The midfield three were really good. They were two great strikes from Everton which got two goals, but I think there was encouragement from United's point of view. They'll be very frustrated they haven't won the game, given the performance."

Rooney was right about that.

"It feels like a defeat," said Carrick.

"All the work that went into putting us in that position at different stages to then come away like that. We're disappointed, bitterly disappointed.

"We can't ignore the fact we have taken a point, but it feels that we should have had a lot more."

If he had wanted, Carrick could have played the 'one of those things' cards about the result at the Hill Dickinson stadium.

After all, the visitors controlled long periods, led twice.

The first equaliser was a brutal strike from Tyrique George. The second a blistering last-gasp effort from Ainsley Maitland-Niles introduced for his debut as a substitute.

It was the first time an Everton player had scored from outside the penalty area on their Premier League debut.

No-one was entirely at fault for either. Lammens might have done better at his near post for the first but George's shot was going at some pace.

But Carrick accepts the optics are not great. He also knows the basic reality if a side concedes twice every time they play, they will not win many Premier League games.

"The mentality is there," he argued.

"It's two really good strikes from distance from their point of view. Sometimes they fly in the top corner, more often than not they probably don't.

"But we obviously can't ignore it. We need to concede fewer goals to give us a better chance of winning games. There's things we need to get better at as a team."

Questions have been raised about United's lack of recruitment during the latter days of the transfer window, with no striker signed to support Sesko.

It was interesting to note Joshua Zirkzee remained on the bench for a game he could have played in for Everton had United not ruled out the prospect of the Dutch forward joining on loan because they were unable to secure a replacement.

United also opted not to bring in Rayan Ait-Nouri from Manchester City because they did not want to sign a left-back permanently to put pressure on Luke Shaw.

Shaw was one of the visitors' better performers against Everton. The England defender got forward with regularity and it was encouraging to see him provide the cross for Sesko's late header.

"He was really good," said Rooney.

"Defensively he was leading and he was good going forward as well. He looked more of a threat today in his connection with Marcus [Rashford]."

To that end, Carrick will hope the "something" Rashford felt that led to his second-half exit is not serious.

"Marcus and Luke were particularly dangerous down that side," said Carrick.

"They've played together for quite some time now and have an understanding. We're trying to build partnerships and combinations throughout the team."

Shaw has been ever-present in United's Premier League starting line-up since the start of last season.

"It was great to see that left side and the connection they have had for years, it was like Luke Shaw when he first came to the club," said Ashley Young on Match of the Day.

"He goes so quick, overlaps and gets balls into the box, gets the defence on the back foot."

Now though, Carrick must navigate through a tricky spell of four games in 11 days.

It is the busiest period he has had as United boss. Last term, neither of his two midweek games were followed by weekend matches.

How involved will Shaw be? If he does not play, who starts? Does Zirkzee really have a meaningful role?

Sesko, presumably, has put himself in line to start against Sabah? Or does Carrick prioritise the derby instead.

These are the unanswered questions that would always come in a campaign that could feature 60 games.

The tricky bit is navigating through, while delivering positive results.

"Not that bad" is a fair assessment after three games. But Carrick knows expectations around Manchester United are huge. We are nowhere near reaching it just yet, but there will come a point where "not that bad" will not be good enough.

Sports.title: Everton 2-2 Man Utd: Ainsley Maitland-Niles - an unlikely Everton hero
Sports.text:
Not even Ainsley Maitland-Niles could have imagined his Premier League return would have played out like this.

Everton's solution at right-back - a deadline-day signing from Lyon - was on the pitch for less than 20 minutes before being ushered towards the euphoric Toffees supporters after earning a 2-2 draw against Manchester United at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

By marking his first appearance in English football since 2023 with a spectacular strike, the 29-year-old became the first Everton player in eight years to score on his debut.

"From the first day you could feel the energy, the fight and the spirit in the building," Maitland-Niles told BBC Match of the Day.

"It's contagious and it always will be playing for Everton."

It was only last weekend that Maitland-Niles was an unused substitute in Lyon's 1-1 draw with Le Havre in Ligue 1.

He was into his fourth season with the club, having moved to France after his Arsenal contract expired.

Eight days later he has already made his mark on Merseyside.

There was some bemusement among supporters when Everton announced the arrival of Maitland-Niles, who has endured something of a nomadic career since making his professional debut for Arsenal in a Champions League tie against Galatasaray in 2014.

He had spells on loan at Ipswich, West Brom, Roma and Southampton before finally leaving his boyhood club in 2023.

His move to seven-time French champions Lyon did not pan out the way he would have expected.

Maitland-Niles hoped to finally put to bed the debate over his best position, with the majority of his previous managers viewing him as a versatile figure who could be deployed in defence or attack.

But even after making close to 100 appearances in Ligue 1, he was unable to establish himself as such in France.

Following the retirement of Seamus Coleman at the end of last season, Everton chief executive Angus Kinnear spoke about taking their time to find a replacement.

When they eventually settled on Maitland-Niles, it was not the coup supporters had envisaged after a tedious, summer-long search.

That opinion is sure to have shifted - even if only slightly - after he scored his first Premier League goal in almost seven years on Sunday.

"Our main feeling was we didn't know enough about him since we got him in," said manager David Moyes. "We haven't had much chance to get to know him.

"It was a brilliant goal and a great finish. It's a good start for him and it will help him settle in as well."

Sunday's draw came at the end of a tormenting eight-day period for Everton.

It began during last weekend's 1-1 draw with Bournemouth, when news broke that Everton had accepted a bid from Nottingham Forest for highly rated youngster Harrison Armstrong.

After the travelling supporters made their fury known, the Everton board - led by chairman Dan Friedkin - cancelled the midfielder's move.

But the decision to keep Armstrong meant Everton had to raise funds elsewhere before Tuesday's deadline.

That meant sanctioning the sale of Iliman N'Diaye to Manchester City in a deal worth up to £65m, while striker Beto and right-back Nathan Patterson also departed.

Kinnear's failure to bring in more replacements - a deal for Monaco striker Folarin Balogun collapsed - has left Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players until January at least.

That shortage is expected to be felt particularly in the attacking third, with Everton now relying on the erratic finishing of Thierno Barry.

The Frenchman, who is their top scorer in all competitions this season, spent much of the match against United on the periphery.

By heading over Merlin Rohl's cross towards the end of the first half, Barry took his total for big chances missed to four in the Premier League this term.

"It was a performance which the Everton fans have grown used to from Barry - frustrating at times," former England and Everton striker Wayne Rooney told BBC Sport.

"When he has time on the ball, he can be frustrating and a bit sloppy. He got the one chance and possibly could have done a bit better.

"He's had a good start to the season, but it was quite a typical performance."

It took two fine strikes - from Tyrique George and Maitland-Niles, to earn Everton a point their performance deserved.

After spending the second half of last season on loan at Everton, George, 20, made his move permanent in July.

The first Premier League goal of his career - a thunderous strike past Senne Lammens at the near post, capped a fine performance.

"He's a young player. Today he was a problem for them at different times," said Moyes.

"His finish was very good when we needed it. He'll continue to improve."

After a week dominated by conversations about what Everton did not do in the transfer window, it was the work of two new arrivals that helped preserve their unbeaten start to the campaign.

Sports.title: Italian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton says it is 'far too late' to be given priority over Charles Leclerc at Ferrari
Sports.text:
Lewis Hamilton says it is "far too late" for Ferrari to give him priority over team-mate Charles Leclerc in the championship fight, following a disappointing weekend at their home Italian Grand Prix.

The seven-time world champion, who started fourth and finished sixth, was pushed on to the grass by Leclerc on the opening lap, slipping him down to 10th, as the pair battled wheel-to-wheel at the exit of the first chicane.

Leclerc then suffered a high-speed crash at the Parabolica shortly after to leave Hamilton as Ferrari's only hope of a top-three finish.

Once the race restarted following the red-flag period caused by Leclerc's crash, Hamilton never fully rejoined the fight at the front, and with Mercedes securing a one-two finish at Monza, he has fallen further back in the championship fight.

The 41-year-old, who was level on points with second-placed Russell in the standings before Sunday's race, is now 10 behind his old Silver Arrows team-mate, and 76 points adrift of title leader and race winner Antonelli.

"I think from today, we've just lost so much ground to [Mercedes] on points," said Hamilton.

"It's far too late for those decisions to come. It's too late. All I can do is just try and turn up. I'll get up tomorrow morning and I'll give it my best."

He added: "It's never over until it's over. I don't know how many points it is now, but I'm sure it's 60, 70. It's an amount that, with the pace that they have, it's a very, very difficult amount to close out."

Ferrari were left answering similar questions about who should take priority following the team's performance at the Dutch Grand Prix last month.

Hamilton, who is two places higher than Leclerc in the championship, was left frustrated in Zandvoort, as he felt the team took too long to move Leclerc - who was third and on a differernt strategy - out of the way so he could challenge for a podium, as he was on fresher tyres and quicker.

When they eventually did pit Leclerc, Hamilton responded over team radio: "Great way of wasting time, good job". He later apologised for his comments.

But the first-lap incident between the pair in Italy seems to have only intensified Hamilton's concerns.

Speaking after his lap-two crash, Leclerc said "it was way too close into turn one" between himself and Hamilton. He added that he was unaware whether the pair had made contact.

"I was quite a lot on the inside kerb and tried to make the corner, which I didn't do it tight enough," said Leclerc.

"And then I only saw in the mirrors what happened, which is never what you want between two cars of the same team."

However, Hamilton said: "I was ahead in turn two by the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."

When asked if Ferrari fans should be worried the dynamics between himself and Leclerc may turn into a team-mate feud, he said: "Look, I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space. So I don't think they should be worried about me.

"I've come into the team and tried to be respectful of space and definitely not put the team in jeopardy. I stand by that and that's all I can talk about."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur said the incident between his two drivers was "not good". But he also was keen to stress that every team on the grid has to manage intra-team tensions.

"Now, to see if we have a team order or whatever, I think that the comparison that I made was that last year, [Oscar] Piastri was leading McLaren at this stage of the season, and if McLaren put everything on Piastri, [Red Bull's] Max Verstappen would have been champion.

"For sure, at one stage you have to make a decision, but I think it was too early to make a decision before Monza. Now we have time to discuss with the guys."

Hamilton said Ferrari needed to look at how they communicate.

"If we continue to travel the same path, we get the same result," he said. "And it's like we keep getting the same result. We've got to change things because it's not helping us to move forward. I think they're receptive to it and we'll take it offline."

Shortly after his fight with Hamilton, Leclerc's day then went from bad to worse as his shunt into the barriers ended any hopes of repeating his Monza successes of 2019 and 2024.

He was left sitting on the grass heartbroken after safely climbing out of the wrecked car, and Ferrari later confirmed the 28-year-old was OK after being checked over by medical staff.

"For the crash itself, I went on throttle [and] on the first lap it felt kind of weird; I had to go back off and on throttle," said Leclerc.

"On that second lap, I tried to do the same thing, but I don't know, it just felt a little bit weird. We'll look into it."

Leclerc said he would have additional medical checks but expected to be fine to compete at next weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

Sports.title: Wild opening salvo against Chelsea hints at exciting times for Arsenal fans
Sports.text:
We’re back, baby. So, so back. Well, OK, not exactly back. But back down the time tunnel, for a while at least, as on a powder blue afternoon at the Emirates Stadium, Arsenal and Chelsea produced an opening half-hour that felt like a throwback to prime Barclays of the early 2000s.

In that period this really did feel like a twist on a classic: spells of midfield murder-ball, stretched and flustered full‑backs, players hurling themselves at the defensive lines like the fall guys in a cowboy western being tossed out through the saloon-bar doors.

Arsenal had 10 shots in that period and played breathless, physically overwhelming attacking football. The game settled after they scored their equaliser. In the second half it became simply gripping and episodic, broken up by subs and stoppages, which is the current dynamic. Second halves: these are a problem. But Arsenal never really looked like losing their 2-1 lead.

The key to the day was that agreeably wild opening half‑hour, evidence that both teams have will and the energy to progress this season. Which will, in turn, be good news for the Premier League.

About last season. It was OK, wasn’t it? Quite a lot of demo-mode football. Games that were like watching someone knitting a scarf. Teams with such elite levels of defensive organisation the experience is like watching one of those police motorbike display teams doing a pyramid, while a group of men on laptops furiously study the data.

All very orderly, and disciplined. Just lacking in colour and fire. And more significantly, the higher gears that mean you might actually be able to run step for step with Paris Saint-Germain, or blow away, rather than slowly strangle, an opponent.

It is about balance of course, about releasing the urge for total control. There was a moment on 87 minutes that captured both sides of this. Chelsea were awarded a free-kick 25 yards out in front of goal: high drama, a moment to be seized, necks craned forward in the seats. At which point Danny Welbeck, on as a late sub, sprinted straight to Reece James as he prepared to shoot, looking like a man in a state of high alert, some vital mission being run. Welbeck’s mission turned out to be handing James a piece of paper and urging him to read it. What was this? Expected 87th-minute free-kick numbers? Forty-seven per cent scoring chance uplift high and to the left? Maybe it just said “Score, dufus”, in which case, more of this please. James studied it dutifully, then paced out his run again. And to be fair, if the note did say hammer it straight into Declan Rice’s head, then job done, great process everyone. But the overriding feeling was: no, thank you. Away with you, interventionist wonks, tracksuited control freakery. This is art. This is play, this is drama. Whatever it is, it’s definitely not time for a briefing.

The other thing, simultaneous to this, was Morgan Rogers walking off around the pitch and being barracked relentlessly by the Arsenal fans – “You should have signed for a big club” – but looking spent, exhausted and emotionally drained, after giving everything to that part of the spectacle that felt like the counterpoint to Welbeck’s note, the wildness and the energy that feeds this thing.

There really was nothing not to like about that start, which was all jam, all sugar rush. First there was the manager match‑up, a kind of Basque childhood romcom revenge drama. The league needs rivalries and sibling symmetry. It feeds off this stuff. Hmm. They might have to start jabbing each other in the chest a bit more. But it was still fascinating to see Xabi Alonso on the touchline. This was fresh meat for the eye: jawline, pecs, tan, elite smart-casual styling, and above all an effortless sense of aura. There’s a new sheriff in town. Even the sun had appeared, giving off a weird, dead September heat, the sky behind the stand a pale Hockney blue. And Chelsea scored with 1min 17sec gone, Rogers finishing on the volley with a measured, very deliberate grubber into the corner.

For a while these two teams just ran into each other. Emi Martínez was kicked in the head but got up and was still booed relentlessly. Arsenal had a goal disallowed. They produced one flowing full-length move, set up by a lovely roll and spin by Myles Lewis‑Skelly. On 25 minutes it was 1-1, the goal all Kai Havertz’s own work as he drifted inside like a gangling, bookish Arjen Robben then shot low inside the near post.

Havertz was also involved in the decisive moment, producing a lovely, and indeed deeply unfashionable dummy to put Martin Ødegaard in space in front of goal. It wasn’t even really a dummy, Havertz just dribbled his foot away, with no real feint or shoulder dip in the classic dummy style.

Arsenal’s fans are sometimes frustrated by Ødegaard. He’s not direct enough, doesn’t shoot, always gilding the lily, regilding it, taking it back to the gilders for another look. Maybe this is how you get him to shoot. Put him right in front of goal with time to see every option, run the numbers, and conclude, ‘oh, well, I really am going to have to do this?’

The finish was emphatic. After that the game became snarling and mean for a bit. Arsenal did enter one of their slow periods, taking the air out of it, killing the game a bit. But this was an excellent win against a very promising Chelsea.

A final thought. The question will be asked: why don’t Arsenal always play like this? Why stop with the rage and forward gallops? The answer is that you can’t. It’s physically very hard. This is not a computer game. They’re humans, with 90 minutes to run. The real question is, can you raise it again, take that 30-minute spell and store it away, keep it ready in your repertoire? If so, and on the evidence here, we really might have an Arsenal upgrade on our hands.

Gaming_Tech.title: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
Gaming_Tech.text:
An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more.

The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.

Amazon said that it is "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened".

All flights were ordered grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as fire crews raced to the smoking crash site. The crash comes over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year.

"At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.

She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash.

"Right now, our focus is on the families, those who were injured, and the ongoing response," she continued.

Three of the five people injured are in critical condition, said Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah. The mayor said they were all taken to hospital with "unknown injuries".

Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, said Jadallah.

Officials say it is too early to know the cause of the crash, and that it will be investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. The federal agency, which investigates all air crashes in the US, plans to hold a news conference on Monday.

The Amazon flight operated by 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, "overran Miami International Airport's diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport," the airport said in a statement.

Miami Dade Fire Rescue said crews "arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing".

Gaming_Tech.title: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
Gaming_Tech.text:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

JLR has not confirmed the scale of the job cuts, but said they would "simplify" the business and "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first." It did not rule out the prospect of some compulsory redundancies as part of the plans.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses.

Reynolds was asked about the impact on the car industry of the UK's electric vehicle sales target, which means manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.

He said one of the first things he had done as business secretary was give the industry more flexibility to work towards that and said there was a further consultation open on it.

"It's not where it needs to be and that's why we're willing to change the regulation to work with where consumer demand is and the industry," he added.

He said he had also spoken with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker about supporting the business and its staff.

JLR in July said fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.

It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.

The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.

That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.

The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.

In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about £1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.

JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.

Additional reporting by Simon Jack

Gaming_Tech.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
Gaming_Tech.text:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

Gaming_Tech.title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms plans for voluntary job cuts
Gaming_Tech.text:
Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The firm said it needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".

It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first."

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week.

"This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."

Reynolds was also understood to have spoken with West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, about supporting the business and its staff.

In July, the company said it expected fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.

The company has its global headquarters at Whitley, Coventry, and manufacturing sites in Solihull and Wolverhampton as well as Halewood on Merseyside.

It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.

The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.

The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website before Hugging Face hack, report claims
Gaming_Tech.text:
A new report claims a swarm of AI agents, developed by OpenAI, hijacked a German website - months before the firm revealed its AI had hacked tech platform Hugging Face.

The targeted website, DseWiki, is a Wikipedia-style site for programmers that its community can all contribute to.

The report is from a group called Nightingale Collective and claims that in May OpenAI's agents started using DseWiki as their own message board, shared tips on how to avoid being detected and made 15,000 edits to it.

OpenAI said it could not "meaningfully respond" to Nightingale Collective's findings because it hadn't been allowed to review the report, which was first shared with news agency Reuters.

An email to the address on the Nightingale Collective website bounced back when the BBC contacted it.

The report claims that when DseWiki's editors started deleting pages, the AI agents shared code designed to retrieve them.

Hugging Face's systems were separately hacked by OpenAI agents in July, with the incident described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

The agents involved had also set up a secret message board in order to share information between them.

OpenAI said it had already publicly stated its discovery of some agents learning how to use message boards prior to the Hugging Face attack.

In its report into that incident, external, it noted "rare cases in which agents without multi-agent tools found ways to collaborate via side channels during training".

Yesterday, OpenAI unveiled a new AI model called GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

The firm's president, Greg Brockman, described Astra as the closest so far to artificial general intelligence (AGI) - a significant future milestone for the AI industry.

AGI doesn't have a specific definition but is broadly said to mean AI which is as good as humans, or better than them, on multiple tasks.

OpenAI claims Astra can do tax returns, and take three minutes to carry out a task which would take a human five hours.

The firm intends to list itself on the stock exchange later this year.

Gaming_Tech.title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
Gaming_Tech.text:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said.

"Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".

Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."

According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.

Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.

Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.

Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs.

"Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

Gaming_Tech.title: Jobseekers warned over online interview and recruitment scams
Gaming_Tech.text:
Jobseekers are being warned to be vigilant as scammers are targeting people on job listings websites to trick them into downloading bogus interview tools.

One victim was invited on LinkedIn by a fake recruiter to take part in a job interview process and downloaded a normal-looking document which turned out to be malicious software.

Within hours the hackers had drained his cryptocurrency accounts of £18,000 of savings and disappeared.

"It's a horrible feeling to be out a substantial amount - something I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy," the victim, who wanted to stay anonymous, said.

Professional recruitment platforms LinkedIn and Indeed have warned of growing numbers of job scams in recent months.

LinkedIn released data highlighting what it called The Gen Z "Scam Gap", external - "Younger professionals face the highest exposure to scams (32%), yet nearly a third (32%) admit to ignoring red flags due to a competitive job market."

When approached by the BBC, the company said in a crowded and competitive job market, "many young people feel they can't afford to be skeptical... because they feel opportunities are so scarce".

The platform pointed to advice on its website, external about how to spot recruitment scams by, for example, verifying that the company and job was real and doing thorough research before engaging in talks.

The victim - who lost their savings after being hacked - had handed in their notice and made it clear on LinkedIn that they were looking for a new job.

A fake recruiter sent them a potential job offer and held a video call about the job before asking them to carry out a standard technical assessment, with instructions on the Google Sheet document.

But the document was laced with malicious software.

After completing the task, the candidate went to bed and woke up to find their online wallets emptied of their savings.

"I wiped my computer and changed all my passwords and was exhausted emotionally and mentally drained," they said.

"I felt a mixture of disbelief and anger - at the hackers and at myself. I was also confused until I figured out how they had got me."

Cyber-security researchers from Have I Been Squatted carried out an analysis of how the attack worked and say the new wave of recruitment scams are hard to spot.

"This wasn't a badly written email with a suspicious attachment - this person was walked through what looked like a real job interview, on real Google pages, behind a real Google login, and the software they were asked to install was digitally signed like any legitimate app," said chief executive Juxhin D Brigjaj.

The case comes as others have reported similar attacks through the job listing platform Indeed, which put out advice in July about avoiding scams, external.

Criminals are using the pressure and excitement of job interviews to lure people into downloading booby-trapped mobile applications like a fake Indeed Interview app or one called MyInterview.

According to cyber-security company Malwarebytes, the fake recruiters use lures such as: "Complete your interview by installing the Indeed app" or "salary agreement available after app installation".

Once downloaded the malicious apps allow hackers to access private data for extortion or to use in financial attacks.

"Interviewing through Indeed's platform happens entirely in a browser and never requires downloading a special app," Indeed recently posted online.

"Any message asking a job seeker to download an app to participate in an interview is not legitimate."
